nodes.alt: Original diagram: a vertical glass tube containing water, with a solenoid wound around its lower section and a current source connected to the coil.

children.text: A solenoid of length \(\ell=20\,\mathrm{cm}\) is wound around a vertical, cylindrical test tube made of glass, filled with water. The solenoid is thermally insulated from the water. The height of the water level is approximately \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\) above the upper end of the solenoid, the diameter of the test tube is \(1\,\mathrm{cm}\), the number of turns of the coil is \(N=6000\). The atmospheric pressure is \(p_0=101\,\mathrm{kPa}\), the temperature of water is \(293\,\mathrm K\). Magnetic susceptibility of water is \(\chi\equiv\mu_r-1=-9.04\times10^{-6}\). Vacuum permeability \(\mu_0=12.57\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{H/m}\).

The current in the solenoid is slowly increased until the water starts boiling inside the coil. At which current strength would this happen? Make reasonable approximations when needed. Note that the required current strength might be slightly too large for the present technology.

children.text: Magnetic field gives rise to magnetization of water molecules, i.e. each of the molecules becomes a magnetic dipole. An inhomogeneous magnetic field exerts a force on a magnetic dipole. Water molecules, being diamagnetic, are pushed away from the region of stronger magnetic field. Water reaches a state of mechanical equilibrium where the magnetic force is balanced by a force due to the pressure gradient. Hence, in mechanical equilibrium, regions with stronger magnetic field correspond to smaller pressures. When the current in the solenoid is increased, the pressure differences grow, and at a certain moment, a region will appear where the pressure is smaller than the saturation pressure of the water vapour. This is the moment when water starts boiling.

To begin with, let us discuss possible reasonable approximations. First, we can neglect the water-column pressure, which is only 2 to 4 percent of atmospheric pressure. Second, the saturation pressure of water vapour under normal conditions is also much smaller than atmospheric pressure and therefore can be neglected. Thus boiling starts when the pressure drop due to the magnetic field becomes equal to \(p_0\).

solution.text:
2. Solenoid
Magnetic field gives rise to magnetization of water molecules, i.e. each of the molecules becomes a magnetic dipole. An inhomogeneous magnetic field exerts a force on a magnetic dipole. Water molecules, being diamagnetic, are pushed away from the region of stronger magnetic field. Water reaches a state of mechanical equilibrium where the magnetic force is balanced by a force due to the pressure gradient. Hence, in mechanical equilibrium, regions with stronger magnetic field correspond to smaller pressures. When the current in the solenoid is increased, the pressure differences grow, and at a certain moment, a region will appear where the pressure is smaller than the saturation pressure of the water vapour. This is the moment when water starts boiling.
To begin with, let us discuss possible reasonable approximations. First, we can neglect the water-column pressure, which is only 2 to 4 percent of atmospheric pressure. Second, the saturation pressure of water vapour under normal conditions is also much smaller than atmospheric pressure and therefore can be neglected. Thus boiling starts when the pressure drop due to the magnetic field becomes equal to \(p_0\).
We need to relate the pressure difference caused by the magnetic field to the magnetic-field strength. If a region with magnetic field \(B\) is filled with water, the magnetic-field energy density is \(B^2/(2\mu_r\mu_0)\). If there is no water, the energy density is \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\). We can ascribe the energy-density difference
\[\Delta w=(\mu_r^{-1}-1)B^2/(2\mu_0)\]
to the interaction of water and magnetic field. Consider the following thought experiment. We push away a small volume \(V\) of water from the neighbourhood of a point \(P\) where the magnetic-field strength is \(B\). The displaced water fills a narrow layer at the top of the water surface of equal volume. Assuming the magnetic field is negligibly small at the top, the total interaction energy is reduced by \(V(\mu_r^{-1}-1)B^2/(2\mu_0)\). When pushing away water from \(P\), we perform mechanical work \(pV\), where \(p\) is the pressure at \(P\). At the upper surface, the moving interface performs mechanical work \(p_0V\), so the net work performed by water is \(V(p_0-p)\). Energy conservation gives
\[V(\mu_r^{-1}-1)\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}=V(p_0-p),\qquad p_0=p+(\mu_r^{-1}-1)\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.\]
This derivation is analogous to that of Bernoulli's law. The equality can be interpreted as a modified Bernoulli law for zero speed where the gravitational potential-energy density \(\rho gh\) is replaced by \((\mu_r^{-1}-1)B^2/(2\mu_0)\), the energy density of magnetic interaction. Since \(\mu_r^{-1}-1=-\chi/\mu_r\approx-\chi\),
\[p_0-p=-\frac{\chi B^2}{2\mu_0}.\]
As discussed above, the boiling condition is \(p\approx0\), hence
\[B=\sqrt{-2\mu_0p_0/\chi}.\]
Finally, using the magnetic-field strength inside a long solenoid, \(B=\mu_0IN/\ell\),
\[I=\frac\ell N\sqrt{\frac{2p_0}{-\chi\mu_0}}=4.4\,\mathrm{kA}.\]
